input.question: In contact sports when bodychecking an opponent, do you gain extra force by leaving your feet?
input.ground_truth: Being off the ground does not itself make you have extra force, but rather it is having a lot of force that tends to make you leave the ground. After all, when you are running or jumping you are pushing off of the ground, and the more powerfully you push, the further from the ground you tend to go. A bigger problem with being in the air is that you have no ability to stop yourself from moving in the direction you are moving, which means that you are at a much higher risk of a collision than if you are on the ground and still able to maneuver yourself.

response.prediction:
Okay! Let’s imagine you’re playing a game where you can bump into your friend gently (like in hockey or soccer).

If you want to bump your friend and make the bump stronger, you can do two things:

1. **Stay on your feet and push with your legs.**  
   This is like walking and then giving a little push with your feet on the ground.

2. **Jump and then bump.**  
   If you jump into the bump, you use the push from the ground that helped you jump, plus your own body moving in the air. That makes your bump a little stronger because you have more “oomph” from the jump.

So, **leaving your feet (jumping) can give you a little extra force** when you bodycheck, because you get a boost from jumping and then using that energy to bump into your friend. But you have to be careful not to hurt anyone!
